Basic Nutrition Guidance for Families
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Good nutrition means eating a variety of foods in the right amounts to keep the body healthy, active, and able to fight illness. What a family eats every day has a direct effect on the growth of children, the strength of working adults, and the health of pregnant women and elderly family members.
A healthy diet does not need to be expensive or complicated. It simply means eating a balanced mix of foods, avoiding excess sugar, salt, and oil, and making the most of foods that are already available locally. Poor nutrition, whether from eating too little or eating an unbalanced diet, can lead to problems such as poor growth in children, weakness, low immunity, and a higher risk of long-term diseases like diabetes and heart disease in adults.
This document offers simple, general guidance on healthy eating for the whole family, along with information on why nutrition matters and how local food traditions can support good health.
Key Practices
Eat a Variety of Foods
Include foods from different groups at each meal: cereals (rice, wheat, millets), pulses (dal, beans), vegetables, fruits, and where possible, milk, eggs, or meat
Eat a mix of colours of fruits and vegetables, as different colours provide different vitamins and minerals
Use a combination of cereals and pulses (such as rice and dal) together, as this improves the quality of protein in the meal
Balance the Plate
Fill about half the plate with vegetables and fruits
Include a portion of whole grains such as rice, wheat, or millets
Add a portion of pulses, beans, eggs, fish, or meat for protein, based on what is available and affordable
Use oil and ghee in moderation rather than in excess
Limit Salt, Sugar, and Oil
Reduce added salt in cooking and avoid excess salty snacks, pickles, and papad
Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and packaged snacks
Choose boiled, steamed, or lightly cooked foods over deep-fried foods when possible
Special Attention for Vulnerable Groups
Young children need frequent, small meals with a variety of foods to support healthy growth
Breastfeeding is recommended for infants in the first months of life, along with timely introduction of a variety of foods as the child grows
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra nutritious food, including iron- and protein-rich foods, to support their own health and their child's growth
Elderly family members should be encouraged to eat soft, easily digestible, nutrient-rich foods and to stay well hydrated
General Habits
Eat meals at regular times and avoid skipping meals
Drink enough clean water through the day
Wash fruits and vegetables well before eating or cooking
Where possible, grow a small kitchen garden with vegetables and leafy greens for fresh, affordable nutrition
Why It Matters
Good nutrition supports healthy growth in children, helps prevent illness, and gives the body strength for daily work and study. Malnutrition, whether from too little food or an unbalanced diet, can affect a child's physical growth and ability to learn, and can weaken the immune system, making infections more likely.
At the same time, unhealthy eating habits, such as excess salt, sugar, and oily food, contribute to long-term health problems including high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. Following a balanced diet from childhood through old age helps reduce the risk of these conditions later in life.
Proper nutrition is especially important during pregnancy, early childhood, and adolescence, as these are periods of rapid growth and development. Good nutrition in these stages has a lasting impact on health across a person's lifetime.
Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha has a rich tradition of local foods that can support good nutrition when eaten in the right balance. Everyday staples such as rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, and leafy greens form the foundation of a healthy Odia diet and are widely accessible across the state.
Traditional millets such as ragi (mandia), suan, and kangu are climate-resilient, nutrient-rich grains that have long been part of the diet in Odisha's tribal and rainfed regions
The Government of Odisha's Millet Mission (Shree Anna Abhiyan) works to revive millet farming and encourage the inclusion of millets in everyday meals, school Mid-Day Meals, and Anganwadi nutrition programmes
Seasonal, locally grown vegetables and fruits are often more affordable and fresher than store-bought or processed alternatives, and are encouraged as part of daily meals
Anganwadi centres and ASHA workers provide guidance and supplementary nutrition support for young children, pregnant women, and lactating mothers under national nutrition programmes
Families are encouraged to combine traditional foods like rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, and millets to create balanced, affordable, and locally accessible meals
Making the most of these local foods is an easy and culturally familiar way for Odisha families to support good nutrition at home.
Source Basis
This document is based on general, publicly available health awareness information from the following organisations. It has been written in simple language for awareness purposes and paraphrased in original wording; it does not quote any source directly.

National Health Mission (NHM) – nhm.gov.in
